title: Sikhism: one creator
hook: the Guru Granth Sahib opens with the Mool Mantar: one creator, truth is the name (Japji)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ramadan, the fasting month. Your line was hunger teaches. What did the skipped snack teach you? Day two hundred seventy-four, and a new visit: Sikhism.

Most holy books begin with a story, or a greeting, or a prayer. The Sikh scripture begins with a number. Before a single word, on the very first page, there's the numeral one, written in Gurmukhi, the Punjabi script. You'll see that symbol everywhere in Sikh life: over the doors of gurdwaras, on car dashboards, on pendants, even tattooed on forearms. It's the first thing the first Guru wanted anyone to know. Today, on our visit to Sikhism: Ik Onkar, and the few lines that follow it.
screen: `A HOLY BOOK THAT STARTS WITH A NUMBER.` → `OVER DOORS, ON DASHBOARDS.` → `IK ONKAR.`

segments.voice: Sikhism begins with Guru Nanak, born in 1469 in Punjab, in what is now Pakistan. Sikh tradition says that as a young man he disappeared into a river for three days and came out with a message about one God, and spent the rest of his life traveling and singing it. His words, and those of the Gurus after him and of other saints, were gathered into the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs honor as their living Guru. It opens with the Mool Mantar, the root verse. Here is its sense, line by line; the Punjabi is compact, so this is a paraphrase. Ik Onkar: there is one creator, one being, present in everything. Sat Naam: whose name is truth. Karta Purakh: the creator. Nirbhau: without fear. Nirvair: without hate. Akal Murat: beyond time. Ajuni: never born. Saibhang: existing by itself. Gur Prasad: known by the Guru's grace. Nine short phrases, and a whole picture of God. Look at the first word again. Ik is the numeral one, written as a digit, not spelled out, as if to make sure no one argues with it. Onkar is a name for the one reality, and the long curving line drawn over the top is often read as that oneness reaching on without end. Sikhs say this one creator isn't far off: the same one is in every person, which is why Sikh teaching insists on the equality of all people, whatever their caste, gender or faith. The Mool Mantar opens Japji Sahib, the prayer many Sikhs recite every morning before dawn.
screen: `GURU NANAK, PUNJAB, 1469.` · `THE MOOL MANTAR: THE ROOT VERSE.` · `WITHOUT FEAR, WITHOUT HATE.` · `IK — THE NUMERAL ONE.` · then, large: `ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the numeral one. Take a pen and a scrap of paper, or trace it with your finger on your palm or the table. Draw it slowly. As you do, breathe out, and let the word one settle in you. Then look at the people you'll see today, in your mind, one by one, and hold the thought that the same one is in each of them. The bell holds the time.
Ik Onkar. One creator: the numeral one that opens the Sikh scripture, the first words of the Mool Mantar. Today's word.
Your line: one. Today, keep your little written one where you'll see it, and when you meet someone who annoys you, remember the same one is in them. Day two hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib, which begins with the Mool Mantar, early each morning, and the Ik Onkar symbol appears over gurdwara doors, in homes and on the first page of the Guru Granth Sahib.
